title: Plus One Linked List
statement:
The linked list `head` stores a non-negative integer in decimal, one digit per node, with the most significant digit in the first node. Add one to that integer and return the head of a linked list that stores the result in the same way.

The input has no leading zeros, except when the integer is zero itself, which is the single node `0`. The result must not have leading zeros either; it may be one node longer than the input (for example when every digit is `9`).
constraints: The number has no leading zeros, except the number 0 itself
notes:
## Intuition

The simple idea copies the digits into an array, adds one from the right with a carry, and builds a new list. But the effect of `+1` is easy to describe directly: the trailing run of `9`s turns into `0`s, and the digit just before that run goes up by one. The list is singly linked, so we cannot walk backwards, but one forward pass can remember the **last digit that is not 9**. If every digit is `9`, a sentinel node holding `0` in front of the head plays that role and becomes the new leading `1`.

## Approach

1. Create `sentinel` with value `0` pointing at `head`, and let `lastNotNine` start at it.
2. Walk the list with `node`; whenever `node.val` is not `9`, set `lastNotNine = node`.
3. Add one to `lastNotNine.val`. It was at most `8`, so no new carry appears.
4. Every node after `lastNotNine` held a `9`; set each of them to `0`.
5. If the sentinel became `1`, the number grew a digit, so return `sentinel`; otherwise return `sentinel.next`.

## Example 1, step by step

The list is `1 → 2 → 3`. The walk sees `1`, `2` and `3`, none of them a `9`, so `lastNotNine` ends on the node `3`. It becomes `4`, there are no later nodes to reset, and the sentinel is still `0`, so the answer is `sentinel.next`: `[1, 2, 4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass to find `lastNotNine` and at most one more over the nines after it.
- Space: O(1): the list is changed in place; only the sentinel is added.

## Pitfalls

- Adding one to the last node alone fails as soon as it is a `9`; the carry must reach the right digit.
- An all-nines number such as `[9, 9, 9]` needs an extra leading node: the answer is `[1, 0, 0, 0]`.
- Do not return the sentinel when it is still `0`, or the answer gains a leading zero.
- Reversing the list twice also works but is longer and easier to get wrong.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sentinel` | extra node holding `0` in front of `head`, used when every digit is `9` |
| `lastNotNine` | the rightmost node whose digit is not `9` |
| `node` | the node being visited during a pass |

narration.2: Put a sentinel holding 0 in front of the list; it absorbs the carry if every digit is 9.
narration.3: So far the sentinel is the rightmost digit known not to be 9.
narration.6: Walk every node of the list from the most significant digit.
narration.7: A digit other than 9 can take the +1 without carrying further.
narration.8: Remember it as the rightmost such digit so far.
narration.13: Add one to the rightmost non-9 digit; it was at most 8, so it stays a single digit.
narration.14: Start at the node right after it.
narration.20: If the sentinel became 1 the number gained a digit, so it is the new head; otherwise skip it.
